title: Do You Truly Motivate or Just Bribe Others to Raise Their Game
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece challenges leaders' heavy reliance on compensation and other external incentives, noting decades of research showing such rewards can actually erode intrinsic motivation even though they demonstrably work in the short term. It doesn't argue for abandoning incentives, but warns that leaders who become overly incentive-focused end up "bribing" people to chase a prize rather than cultivating a higher vision, collaborative spirit, or the satisfaction of ownership. The author points to skill investment, influence, mission, and relationships as alternative motivators that build lasting, intrinsic drive rather than transactional compliance. It closes by urging readers to audit how incentive-dependent their own motivation strategy has become and to consciously diversify it.
points: Compensation and other external incentives reliably work to boost performance, but research shows they can erode intrinsic motivation over time.
Leaders who over-rely on incentives risk perfecting "bribery", attracting behavior toward a prize rather than a shared vision or ownership of the work.
Alternative motivators like skill investment, influence, mission, and relationships build more durable intrinsic drive than compensation alone.
The article recommends leaders audit their own reliance on incentives and deliberately diversify their motivational toolkit.
quotes: Chief among the needs leaders tap into to compel action and inspire higher performance are incentives.
But here’s the irony, for decades research has shown that external rewards, such as compensation, actually diminish the natural and intrinsic motivation people have to do a better job.
Without realizing it, leaders who are too incentive-focused rob people of their intrinsic motivations.

Great leaders do their best to limit their use of incentives and authority to get things done because they know that long-term success depends on team members who are intrinsically motivated to reach for quality results.
No leader wants to think of themselves as bribing others to do their best, but that’s exactly what occurs in a workplace driven primarily through external rewards.
